children.text: Completed in

, this ochre stone fortress church is famous for the façade relief of Saint Christopher clinging to a coconut tree. One of four Philippine baroque churches inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, it makes an easy half-day trip from Iloilo.
Miagao Church's official name is Santo Tomás de Villanueva Parish Church. It stands on a hill facing the town plaza of Miagao, about
40km
southwest of Iloilo City; construction began in
and was completed in
. It's said that villagers, under forced labor, hauled the stone under the supervision of Augustinian friar Francisco Gonzalez and town official Domingo Riovoon.
Miagao Church is often called the "fortress church." In the 18th century, Moro pirate raids were frequent along Panay's southern coast, and after the attacks of
and
the town moved from its old seaside site to the present hill. The walls are about
thick and the foundation about
6m
deep, and buttresses
4m

thick support the walls. However, the monsignor who served as parish priest when the church was restored and inscribed as a UNESCO site explained that the seven buttresses lined up on each side are meant to withstand earthquakes and typhoons rather than serve a military purpose, and that the narrow windows of the bell towers are for ventilation; he also says there is no record of the church ever being attacked after it was completed. So some sources present it as a building that also served for defense, while other interpretations say it did not. The two bell towers on either side differ in height: the west tower (on the left as you face the church) has four stories and the east tower three. The east tower originally had two stories, and a floor was added in

What made Miagao Church world-famous is its front façade. Carved into ochre stone made from a mix of sandstone, limestone, and coral, the central relief shows Saint Christopher carrying the infant Jesus on his shoulder while holding onto a giant coconut tree cast as the "tree of life," surrounded by tropical plants like papaya and guava and figures in traditional Philippine dress. It's regarded as a masterpiece of the country's own "folk baroque" style, blending Spanish baroque with local nature and Chinese and Islamic decorative elements.
The church suffered major damage several times — during the revolution of
, a fire in
, World War II, and an earthquake in
— and was restored in
. It was declared a National Historical Landmark in
, and in

it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site under "Baroque Churches of the Philippines," alongside San Agustin Church in Manila, Paoay Church in Ilocos Norte, and Santa Maria Church in Ilocos Sur. For travelers interested in history and architecture, it's a must-see stop from Iloilo.

Miagao, home to the church, is a coastal town of about 157 km² with a population of roughly 68,000 (2024 census), and with 119 barangays it has more than any other municipality in the Philippines. Most residents speak Kinaray-a, and Hiligaynon is also widely understood. In

the church underwent restoration in which the National Museum cleaned the façade and replaced broken stones with stone from the original quarry; stripping away the cement plaster applied earlier revealed the rough stone texture you see today. Tigbauan, Guimbal, and San Joaquin churches lie along the same road, making Miagao a good hub for a tour of Iloilo's southern churches.

blocks.title: Study the façade relief up close

children.text: Look for Saint Christopher and the coconut tree, the patron saint Santo Tomás de Villanueva above the central door, and the coats of arms and figures on either side. Up close, tropical leaves and flowers are carved in intricate detail.

blocks.title: Compare the two mismatched bell towers

children.text: The four-story and three-story towers were built in different periods. Walk around the side of the church to see the thick walls and buttress structure that reveal its true nature as a fortress church.

blocks.title: Photograph the full façade from the plaza steps

children.text: Looking up from the plaza and the foot of the steps in front of the church frames the whole façade in one shot. The gold tones are richest in the late afternoon, when sunlight hits at a low angle.

blocks.title: The church interior and attending Mass

children.text: The interior is plainer than the exterior, but the cool air created by the high ceiling and thick walls leaves an impression. Attending Sunday Mass gives you a feel for the local faith community.

blocks.title: Salakayan Festival — reenacting the 1754 Moro raid

children.text: The Salakayan Festival, held in the
first week of February
, reenacts in a street dance-drama the day
, when 21 Moro pirate ships attacked the town and were driven off by the residents. It has been held since the
late 1990s
, and being the middle of the dry season, the weather is good too. The dates change every year, so check the municipal government's announcements.

blocks.title: Visit a Miagao hablon weaving workshop

children.text: Miagao is known for hablon, a traditional handwoven fabric. At workshops on the edge of town, you can watch the weaving process and buy a scarf or piece of cloth as a souvenir.

Miagao is home to the main campus of the University of the Philippines Visayas (UP Visayas). Known for its fisheries college, it has a campus where sea and hills come together, pleasant for a stroll. The highlight is the sea goddess statue Diwata ng Dagat, made by National Artist Napoleon Abueva. As it's a school facility, move around quietly during class hours.

blocks.title: The golden altar and the old saint statue

children.text: At the center of the gilded retablo on the main altar is a crucifix, flanked by statues of Saint Joseph and Santo Tomás de Villanueva, with the Santo Niño enshrined at the very top. To the left of the altar is a statue of the Sacred Heart of Jesus, and to the right a statue of the Immaculate Heart of Mary. In a glass case at the back of the church is a statue of Santo Tomás made in the
late 1790s

items.title: If extending it into a full day

children.text: See Tigbauan and Guimbal churches in the morning, have a seafood lunch at a coastal restaurant, then combine Miagao and San Joaquin in the afternoon to complete a tour of Iloilo's southern churches.

items.title: Full-day chartered-vehicle itinerary
items.subtitle: Departing from Iloilo City, a tour of the southern churches

children.text: Leave Iloilo City and head southwest along the national highway (the Iloilo-Antique road).
At Tigbauan Church (Saint John of Sahagún Church), see the interior decorated with colorful stone mosaics.
At Guimbal Church, take in the yellowish stone façade. The church is designated a National Cultural Treasure.
Arrive at Miagao Church and see, in turn, the façade relief, the two bell towers, the buttresses on the side, and the altar inside.
Have lunch around the plaza or at a coastal restaurant.
At the UP Visayas campus, see the Diwata ng Dagat statue and take a stroll.
At a hablon cooperative or workshop you've contacted in advance, watch the weaving process and buy souvenirs.
At San Joaquin Church, see the façade carved with the Battle of Tetuán from the Spanish-Moroccan War of 1860, then look around the Campo Santo (cemetery chapel) across the road.
Head back to Iloilo City, arriving in about
1 hour
Church entry is free, but interior viewing is restricted during Mass. A chartered vehicle is typically for 8 hours with driver and fuel included, so allow plenty of time for lunch and travel.
From Manila to Iloilo International Airport (ILO) takes about
1 hour 10 minutes–1 hour 30 minutes
, with daily nonstop flights by AirAsia, Cebu Pacific, and Philippine Airlines. A one-way fare runs about
depending on season and airline.
The airport is in Cabatuan, northwest of Iloilo City, about
from downtown and about
50km
from Miagao, which takes about
1 hour
by vehicle. The airport van (toward the downtown malls) costs about
per person, and a taxi to downtown about
. Most travelers book a hotel in Iloilo City and make the trip from there.

From the southbound terminal in Iloilo City's Molo district (such as Mohon Terminal) or around the downtown terminal market, take a jeepney, van, or bus bound for "Miagao" or for San Joaquin/Antique. It takes about
1 hour
and costs about
per person.
The church sits right beside the national highway (the Iloilo-Antique road) on the plaza, so telling the driver "Miagao Church" will get you dropped off right in front.
Jeepneys depart every
10–20 minutes
and leave as soon as they fill up. You can also board around the downtown terminal market or at the Ceres Antique terminal, and buses bound for Antique pass right in front of the Miagao town plaza.
By Grab or taxi, it costs about

one way (based on Grab's ₱40 base fare plus about ₱12 per km over roughly 40 km). Since it's outside the city, app bookings may be hard to get. To combine several churches, an 8-hour chartered vehicle with driver (about
, based on operators that include fuel and the driver's meal) is more efficient.
From Cebu, nonstop flights on Cebu Pacific and Philippine Airlines take about
55 minutes
, with several flights every day.
From Bacolod, fast ferries run to Iloilo's downtown port: Weesam Express takes about
1 hour 30 minutes
(about
) and OceanJet about
1 hour
(about
), with several sailings a day. From the port, take a jeepney or taxi to Mohon Terminal and board a vehicle to Miagao.
From Iloilo City, follow the national highway (the Iloilo-Antique road) through Oton, Tigbauan, and Guimbal to Miagao, about
40km
and
40–50 minutes
. The church is right beside the highway, so it's easy to find, though the roadside can get crowded on Sunday Mass days and during festivals.
The area around the church is easy to explore on foot, and a tricycle to the hablon workshop or the university campus costs about
per ride.
The dry season, from
December
to
May
, is good for a visit. Photos come out best from
February–April
, when clear skies are common and the contrast between blue sky and the ochre façade is sharpest. However, the plaza has almost no shade at midday from
March–May
, so it gets very hot — visiting before
or after
is recommended.
From
June
to
November
is the rainy season with frequent afternoon showers, but since this is a half-day trip, there's usually a dry window to fit it in. Typhoons mainly affect the area between
August–November
. During the Christmas season and Holy Week (the week before Easter), church decorations and religious events add more to see, though viewing may be limited during Mass times.
Timing your visit with town events gives you more to see. The Salakayan Festival is held in the
first week of February
, the Hablon Festival runs from
mid-September to September 22
, and
September 22
is the feast day of the patron saint, Santo Tomás de Villanueva. In Iloilo City, the Dinagyang Festival in
late January
(main events on
January 23–25
in 2026) and the Paraw Regatta in
late February to early March
take place in the dry season and fit well into the same trip. During festivals, Iloilo accommodations fill up early and jeepneys get crowded, so book in advance.

Miagao does have a few small guesthouses and beach resorts, but most travelers base themselves in Iloilo City and visit on a half-day trip. Mid-range hotels in Iloilo City run about
a night. If you'd like to enjoy the southern coastal drive, you could also spend a night at a beach resort in Miagao or nearby Guimbal or Tigbauan (about
a night).

Around the church plaza there are local carinderias, bakeries, and snack stalls, good for a light meal. Iloilo's southern coast has fresh seafood, and many coastal eateries serve sinabawang fish soup and grilled shellfish and shrimp. It's also a good idea to head back to Iloilo City and have dinner there — La Paz batchoy or pancit Molo.

Lodging in Miagao ranges from small guesthouses to beach resorts, at roughly US$25–75 (about ₱1,400–4,200) per night. The town's signature souvenir is hablon, a traditional handwoven fabric. The Indahag cooperative (Barangay Indahag), which began as a support program in

and has continued to this day, weaves patadyong cloth, shawls, handkerchiefs, and table runners, and sometimes demonstrates the weaving process. Around the plaza you can find local snacks such as bayi-bayi, made by rolling coconut flesh and pinipig (pounded rice), and ibos, a type of suman. Back in Iloilo City, Deco's, Ted's, and Netong's in La Paz Market are all La Paz batchoy shops that have been around since the
, and Panaderia de Molo in Molo, opened in
, is the oldest bakery in Iloilo and is famous for its Spanish-style biscuits.
As this is a place of worship, avoid sleeveless tops and short shorts, and remove your hat inside. A light long scarf or shirt is handy to have.
A wide-angle lens (or a 0.5x smartphone lens) is useful for capturing the whole façade. Shooting from the road below the plaza also frames the steps in the shot.
With the sun directly overhead at midday, the relief can look flat. The angled light of early morning or late afternoon brings out its depth.
Avoid touring the interior or taking photos during Mass times (especially Sunday morning). Check the church noticeboard or parish announcements before visiting.
Return jeepneys and vans become less frequent from dusk onward, so it's safest to depart around
Buying hablon products directly from a workshop or the village cooperative lets you check the quality and ensures more of the money goes to the weavers.
Sunday Masses are at
, and
, and the weekday default is
. Times may change, so check the parish's Facebook announcements.
Church entry is free, but many jeepneys, snack vendors, and workshops accept cash only, so bring plenty of small ₱20, ₱50, and ₱100 bills. Withdraw cash from an ATM before leaving Iloilo City.
Hablon workshops and cooperatives are places of work, so contact them before visiting to check whether a weaving demonstration is available.

Before it is a tourist attraction, Miagao Church is a working parish where the faithful attend Mass. Entry to the interior and photography may be restricted during Mass, weddings, and funerals, so follow the parish's instructions; people in sleeveless tops or short shorts may be refused entry.
As this is a heritage site, don't touch the façade relief or lean against the wall for photos. Climbing the steps or bell towers without permission is also prohibited.
Drone photography may require permission from the church or local government. Don't fly during events or Mass.
Traffic is heavy along the highway here. Be careful not to stand in the middle of the road for photos.
The plaza is very sunny at midday, so bring water and a hat to avoid heatstroke.
Interior viewing may be restricted during restoration work or religious events, so check the latest notices.

During the rainy season (June–November) and typhoons, flooding along the highway and canceled flights or fast ferries can occur, so check PAGASA weather forecasts and airline and ferry company notices.
